lines: Thunder shook the village square so hard I jumped before the bell did, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked doors, beds, and hiding places after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
By the bell, the thunder made the whole square flinch. I stayed inside and kept away from windows.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked my hiding spot twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have a safe corner to find.
The rain came sideways through a window that usually knows better.
We kept away from the tall trees. They looked nervous too.
I thought the bell rang, but it was thunder wearing the bell voice.
The roof held. I thanked it even though roofs get proud easily.
Every flash made the square bright as noon and twice as strange.
I brought the animals in. They complained, which meant they were alright.
The storm rolled away, but my shoulders have not heard the news.
I found a dry corner and shared it with four people and one wet chicken.
Lightning split a fence post. We are keeping both halves away from arguments.
I checked for sparks after the last strike. Everything only smelled like rain.
The children counted between thunderclaps. Nobody agreed on the numbers.
Water came under the door, so we taught it the way back out with a broom.
The clouds have moved on. I am waiting before I believe them.
Nobody was struck, and that is the best part of the report.
I can handle ordinary weather again. Quiet rain has excellent manners.
I checked roofs and fences for sparks, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I carried the bucket after.
My chores can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could near the bell, then made sure no one was still coughing alone.
The smoke is thinner now, but I keep smelling my sleeves to make sure it is really gone.
We pulled bedding clear before the flames could learn the doorway.
One roof is black now, but everyone who slept under it is breathing.
I kept filling buckets until my arms forgot how to be arms.
The golem broke a burning beam. I stayed useful somewhere much farther back.
We wet the fences so the fire had nowhere new to visit.
I found a child coughing behind a wall and followed the sound.
The flames are out. The hot stones still disagree.
I singed one sleeve and kept the rest of myself. Fair trade.
People brought water from every direction, including directions without wells.
We saved the homes beside it by knocking down what was already lost.
I keep smelling smoke, but now it is only stuck in my hair.
The village looks wounded. At least it is still a village.
Nobody went back for furniture. Furniture can be made less stubborn than people.
We are watching the ashes until morning in case they remember being fire.
The last ember is dark. I checked three times because embers are sneaky.
During a raid, whatever I was doing can wait. Who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but I still keep looking at the road like it might shout again.
We counted living neighbors before doors, beds, and hiding places. That's the only count worth starting with.
<red><bold>Raiders</bold></red> came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the bell and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the bell, I saw fear cross the square. Then I saw courage get there first.
The first horn made everyone freeze. The second made us move.
I hid two children under the same table I planned to use.
An axe hit the door and the whole house held its breath.
The golem took the road. I took everyone else away from it.
Raiders crossed the fields, but they did not cross our last doorway.
I saw neighbors who never agree fight side by side without a word.
The square is quiet now. It feels like the quiet is listening.
We lost walls and windows. We did not lose each other.
I carried arrows to people who knew which end should face forward.
The horn sounded grand from far away. Up close it was only frightening.
We checked every cellar when the fighting stopped. Nobody gets forgotten underground.
I was scared the whole time and useful for some of it.
The raiders left muddy tracks. Good. We can watch them leave twice.
Victory feels less like cheering and more like finally unclenching your hands.
The village survived. Tomorrow we can argue about who repairs the doors.
Night trouble found the door everyone meant to fix tomorrow. It is getting fixed today.
I stayed near the dark between houses and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn made it easier to see who was missing, which is not the same as making it easier.
The monsters came out of the dark like the dark had been hiding teeth.
We are safe enough, but I still look twice at anything shaped like a monster.
A zombie found the fence gap before we did. The gap is not there anymore.
We moved the children into the stone house and counted them by candlelight.
Something rattled at the shutters until the golem made it stop.
I heard an arrow in the dark. That is a sound I never wanted to learn.
The moon was bright enough to show every place a monster might stand.
I kept a torch in one hand and the door latch in the other.
Nobody slept after the attack, even the people who said they did.
We found claw marks beside the well when morning came.
One skeleton stayed outside the torchlight. It was clever, so we were more clever together.
The last groan faded before sunrise. I still waited for the sun.
Every shadow looked alive until the birds started making ordinary noise.
I patched the broken shutter. It is ugly and very closed.
We made it to dawn with all our names accounted for.
I used to like quiet nights. I will like them again after a few quieter ones.
The beds are full, the doors are barred, and morning has finally arrived.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand from my sleeves.
I checked doors, beds, and hiding places, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand got in my sleeves, my mouth, and places sand should not know about. No one is missing, though.
A hard wind teaches a nitwit which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough, but every step sounds crunchy and everyone is blinking too much.
The square vanished behind a wall the color of old bread.
We followed the house walls because the road had disappeared.
I found the bell by bumping into it. It sounded surprised.
The animals pressed together in the barn and refused every opinion.
Sand piled against the doors until opening one became a group decision.
I held a rope between two houses so nobody wandered into the storm.
The wind stole one roof tile and returned six that were not ours.
We poured water carefully. Half of it turned to mud before reaching a mouth.
Everyone is blinking like the village forgot how eyes work.
The storm scraped paint from the shutters and patience from everyone.
I counted voices when I could not see faces.
The air is clear now, but every room has acquired a tiny desert.
I shook out my blanket and made weather indoors.
No one got lost. We are finding the paths again one doorstep at a time.
The wind has stopped shouting. I would like it to remain embarrassed.
Whatever I was doing can wait. Warm hands and clear paths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the bell found shelter.
Cold is sneaky. I am checking on anyone who stopped complaining about it.
I am clearing snow out of my shoes and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now. I am keeping close to smoke, soup, and shoveled paths.
The drifts swallowed the low fences and made the tall ones look uncertain.
I carried soup. Some reached the neighbors and some warmed my sleeves.
We brought the animals close enough to hear them breathing.
One roof sagged, so we cleared it before it could lie down.
The bell rope froze stiff. We thawed it beside the hearth.
I shoveled the same doorway three times. The snow took that personally.
Everyone with a fire shared it. Nobody counted the wood too closely.
I found a mitten in the road with no person attached. We found the person too.
The wind pushed snow under the shutters in tiny rude lines.
I am checking old neighbors first. Proud people get cold quietly.
We marked the wells with poles before the drifts could hide them.
My boots are wet, my nose is red, and all the beds are occupied.
The storm has passed, but the paths still need convincing.
Warm smoke is rising from every chimney we can see.
Nobody froze alone. That is the part I want remembered.
